question.text: A forward contract is best described as:

answer.text: An OTC contract where two parties agree to buy/sell an asset at a specified price on a future date
An exchange-traded standardized contract with clearing corporation guarantee
A contract that gives the buyer the right but not the obligation to buy an asset
A contract to exchange interest rate payments between two parties

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Series XII page 196, a forward contract is a derivative where two parties agree to exchange a specific good at a specific price on a future date. Page 199 confirms forwards are over-the-counter (OTC) contracts with mutually agreed (non-standard) terms and counterparty risk, since they depend on trust between the two parties. The Trap: Exchange-traded standardized contracts are futures, not forwards (pages 200-201). The right without obligation describes options. Exchange of interest payments describes swaps. The distinguishing feature is OTC vs exchange-traded. Note: Focus on the OTC, mutually-agreed, counterparty-risk nature of forwards as set out on Series XII pages 196 and 199.
